 A joint bank account can significantly enhance financial management for married couples. Experts advocate for shared financial responsibilities, which helps avoid imbalances in earnings and investments. This arrangement simplifies expense tracking and can provide potential tax benefits. It's vital to consider legal aspects, such as proper documentation and asset nominations, ensuring that couples are prepared for any unexpected events in their relationship.  Listen ET Online Why a joint bank account is a must for healthy financial well-being of a married couple In India, marriage is often seen as union not just of two individuals but of two families. So, it is important for married couples to plan their finances, whether it is structuring transactions for tax efficiency or protecting against any unforeseen circumstances. This was one of the main points of discussion in ET Wealth Expo 2026, where a panel of experts shared their insight on how married couples can manage their money more efficiently. The panelists include Aditi Sharma, Partner, Khaitan & Co., CA Nitin Kaushik, Founder-Partner, AMKN & Co. Chartered Accountants, Suresh Sadagopan, Founder, Ladder7 Financial Advisories, and Hiten Shah, Tax Partner, EY India.
 Why is a joint bank account a must for the healthy financial well-being of a married couple?
Ladder7 Financial Advisories’ Sadagopan said that he has seen many married couples who have separated their expenses and responsibilities. Sadagopan says that in this model, the couple has pre-decided that the responsibility of a particular expense would be taken care by one of the spouses, and there is a clear segregation of this. For example, one partner pays the house rent, while the other partner pays for monthly groceries. This model may work for some while not for others.
There is another model, which, Sadagopan says, can be disastrous in the eventuality of a break-up, divorce, etc. In this model, one partner spends all his resources to manage the expenses, while the other partner solely invests their money. This results in disparity, and in the eventuality of a divorce, it can lead to adverse financial impact. 
What is the solution to this problem? A joint bank account, says Sadagopan. In this model, both partners put some amount of their money in the joint bank account for running the expenses of the family, and then via the respective spouse’s individual bank account, the investments and other personal expenses are carried out. Sadagopan says that as per this model, the spouses are contributing as per their income level and then making investments in their own name.

 How can married couples optimise their tax liability?
Hiten Shah of EY India says that gifting money to a spouse for investments or other purposes is not recommended, as it triggers the clubbing of income provisions. Shah said that rather than this model, the couple can explore giving loans to each other via proper documentation and ITR (income tax return) declaration. For example, if a couple wants to buy a house in joint names, one partner could extend a loan to the other partner, disclose the loan interest in ITR, and then buy the house jointly.
For using this arrangement, you need proper documentation, and other legal formalities, you may also explore creating an LLP or partnership between spouses, says Shah.
Nitin Kaushik of AMKN & Co Chartered Accountants says that merely gifting money to a spouse creates an income tax liability for the spouse gifting it because of clubbing provisions. Kaushik suggests that giving a loan to a spouse at an interest rate lower than the interest rate being earned from the corpus can result in tax savings.
Kaushik also suggests that couples can gift money to their own parents, who still fall under the definition of relative, and then execute a Will for that invested corpus. Kaushik says that the husband should gift money to his parents and the wife should do that with her parents.
Kaushik also suggests that husbands can contribute to the Public Provident Fund (PPF) and National Pension System (NPS) corpus of the wife, and this can help the couple in creating a big corpus for themselves and also save on income tax.
Aditi Sharma of Khaitan & Co says that when investing in a joint asset like a joint home, joint FD, etc., couples should look beyond the tax-savings aspects and check the ownership angle too and should also plan for an event where you are absent yet the asset remains accessible to the other partner. For example, if every asset in the household is held only in one partner’s name, then if something happens, the other partner may face delays in accessing the asset.
Sharma says that she, in her practice, has seen cases where there are Indian parents with non-resident children; so, a lot of times, due to lack of nomination in their bank accounts, the children lose access to the account and get tangled in legal procedures, which may further delay the whole process.
So, nomination is very important, says Sharma. She advises couples to make a checklist to ensure that the other partner gets continued access to the assets in the event of the other partner’s absence. (Join our ETWealth WhatsApp channel for all the latest updates)
